summary: Lists the requirements for a gateway function that lets two different internet-telephony systems, SIP and H.323, work together. It describes what such an interworking function must do rather than defining a protocol. It is an informational document.

eli5.summary: Two groups of kids speak different languages, so you need a friendly translator standing between them. This memo says what a good translator for two phone-call systems should be able to do.

subtitle: Requirements for bridging two different internet-telephony protocols

tldr.problem: SIP and H.323 are two incompatible protocols for internet telephony, each used by different networks and devices, making cross-network calls impossible without translation.
tldr.mechanism: An Interworking Function (IWF) gateway translates signaling messages, manages registrations, negotiates capabilities, and handles media between the two networks transparently.
tldr.outcome: Users on SIP and H.323 networks can call each other without knowing which system their peer uses, though end-to-end security cannot be guaranteed across the gateway.

facts.label: Call signaling
facts.value: H.225.0 RAS, H.245, Q.931 on H.323 side; SIP on the other side

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Informational (requirements only, not a protocol specification)

facts.label: Role of media
facts.value: Direct endpoint-to-endpoint when possible, IWF relaying when necessary

today: RFC 4123 is an Informational RFC that remains current. It describes requirements for implementers of SIP-H.323 gateways rather than specifying a protocol itself. While SIP has largely displaced H.323 in new deployments, this RFC remains relevant for enterprises and service providers that must support legacy H.323 networks.

sections.title: Why two phone systems need a bridge
sections.content:
The internet has two major systems for making phone calls: SIP (Session Initiation Protocol, used by many modern VoIP services) and H.323 (an older standard used in videoconferencing and some enterprise systems). They speak completely different languages and have different rules for starting calls, negotiating features, and managing connections.

A network operator needs an Interworking Function (IWF), a translator gateway, to let users on one system call users on the other. This RFC describes what such a gateway must do, without defining the exact wire-level translation rules—those are left for implementers.
sections.eli5: SIP and H.323 are like two walkie-talkie networks with different radio frequencies. An IWF is like a repeater radio that listens on one frequency, understands the message, and broadcasts it on the other frequency so both networks can talk to each other.

sections.title: What the interworking function does
sections.content:
An IWF must perform multiple roles to bridge the two worlds:

Registration and address translation: When a SIP user registers with the IWF, the IWF tells the H.323 gatekeeper "I have a user named john.doe who is on the SIP side." Conversely, H.323 users are registered with SIP proxy servers via the IWF. The IWF maintains translation tables to convert between SIP addresses (like user@example.com) and H.323 addresses (like h323:user@gk.example.com).

Call signaling mapping: When an H.323 phone sends a SETUP message to start a call, the IWF converts it to a SIP INVITE. When a SIP user sends an INVITE, the IWF sends SETUP. The IWF maintains state machines on both sides, tracking call phases and translating state transitions.

Capability negotiation: H.323 terminals declare what audio and video codecs they support using H.245 messages. SIP user agents use SDP (Session Description Protocol). The IWF must map these capability descriptions so both sides can agree on a common audio codec, for example G.711 or a more modern codec.

Media channel management: The IWF opens and closes media channels between endpoints, handling unidirectional and bidirectional connections. It should let endpoints exchange media directly when possible, using the IWF only as a gateway when necessary.
sections.eli5: The IWF acts like a receptionist: it writes down who is calling, tells the H.323 side that a SIP person is on the line, tells the SIP side that an H.323 person is calling, figures out what languages both people speak, and makes sure the phone works for both.

sections.title: How the IWF fits into networks
sections.content:
The IWF can be deployed in several configurations. In the simplest setup, an H.323 endpoint calls directly through the IWF to a SIP user agent. In more complex deployments, the IWF sits between H.323 gatekeepers (which manage groups of H.323 terminals) and SIP proxy servers (which manage SIP registrations). The RFC calls this "GK-routed signaling."

The IWF can register SIP user agents with an H.323 gatekeeper by creating a virtual H.323 alias address for each SIP user. It can also register H.323 terminals with SIP registrars when it also acts as an H.323 gatekeeper. The IWF may be deployed as a separate device or integrated into a gatekeeper or SIP server.

An optional Media-Switching Fabric (MSF) within the IWF can relay media streams when direct endpoint-to-endpoint media is not possible. However, the RFC states the IWF should not convert media from one codec to another—if both sides choose incompatible codecs, the call cannot proceed.
sections.eli5: The IWF can stand alone between two phone systems, or it can live inside a phone company's bigger system that manages many users. It uses the same media relay (RTP) that both systems use, so it does not have to translate audio—it just forwards the same audio packets that came from one side to the other.

sections.title: Call signaling flow
sections.content:
A call from an H.323 terminal to a SIP user agent follows this sequence: the H.323 terminal sends a SETUP message through the IWF. The IWF translates this to a SIP INVITE and sends it to the SIP user agent (or SIP proxy). The SIP side responds with 180 RINGING. The IWF converts this to an H.323 Alerting message so the H.323 caller hears a ringback tone. When the SIP user answers with 200 OK, the IWF sends a Connect message to the H.323 side. Both sides then exchange H.245 messages (for H.323) or complete the SIP three-way handshake (with ACK). Finally, both endpoints open media channels and RTP audio flows.

The reverse direction (SIP to H.323) follows the same pattern in mirror: SIP INVITE maps to H.323 SETUP, H.323 Alerting becomes 180 RINGING, and H.323 Connect becomes 200 OK.

The IWF must maintain strict state machines to handle unexpected messages. A message that arrives in the wrong state should be treated as an error, logged, and handled according to protocol rules for the destination side (for example, sending a SIP 4xx error response).
sections.eli5: When an H.323 phone calls a SIP phone, the IWF hears 'beep beep calling' from H.323, converts it to SIP's 'ring ring,' waits for the SIP side to say 'hello,' and tells the H.323 side the call is answered. Then both phones can talk.

sections.title: Trust and security boundaries
sections.content:
An IWF terminates signaling protocols from both sides, which means it breaks end-to-end security. A caller cannot verify that a message signed by the other party actually came from them—it only came from the IWF. Both sides must trust the IWF to correctly authenticate the caller on the other side and to respect the integrity of information.

H.323 uses H.235 for security; SIP uses TLS and S/MIME. The IWF must ensure that if a caller uses H.235 on the H.323 side, the IWF replies with equivalent security (TLS) on the SIP side, and vice versa. The IWF must not accept a 'sips' (secure SIP) request unless it can guarantee H.235 protection on the H.323 side. This prevents a caller from believing they have end-to-end encryption when in fact an unprotected link exists on the other side.

The RFC also requires that the IWF never claim a user is authenticated on one side unless it actually authenticated that user. For example, if a SIP user was not authenticated (sent from an untrusted proxy), the IWF should not use H.323 mechanisms to claim that user's identity has been verified.
sections.eli5: The IWF is like a post office between two secure envelopes. It has to break both seals, read the address, and reseal it. Both envelope senders must trust the post office not to lose the letter or change it. If one side sends an encrypted letter, the post office must make sure the other side also gets it encrypted, otherwise the sender might think it is safe when it is not.

sections.title: DTMF and supplementary services
sections.content:
DTMF (Dual Tone Multi-Frequency) is the system of tones sent when a user presses keypad buttons (like for entering a PIN or credit card number during a call). H.323 carries DTMF using UserInputIndication messages. SIP has multiple mechanisms (in-band audio, SIP INFO messages, or RTP DTMF payload). The IWF must map between these mechanisms reliably.

The RFC also mentions that the IWF may support H.323 supplementary services like call transfer and conferencing, but this is left for further study. The IWF should only process these services if it explicitly supports them.

For overlapped dialing (where a caller enters phone numbers one digit at a time, not all at once), the IWF can use H.323's Setup, SetupAck, and Information messages to let the H.323 side send digits incrementally before committing to a full call.
sections.eli5: When you press buttons on a phone, the IWF has to convert the beep sounds from one system to the beep sounds the other system understands. It also helps with call transfer and holding calls on hold if both systems support those features.
